claims.statement: JFrog documents the JFrog Access Token as a JSON Web Token that serves as the bearer credential for authenticated requests to the JFrog Platform.

sources.supports: "This JSON Web Token (JWT) acts as the primary internal credential for all authenticated interactions" and "It serves as the bearer token for all subsequent requests"
sources.locator: section "The JFrog Access Token: The Canonical Credential"

sources.supports: access tokens can be used as a bearer token in the Authorization header; since 7.21.1 access tokens are scoped tokens

claims.statement: JFrog documents that an access token can be used as a bearer token in the Authorization header of a request (Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>), for example to the platform ping endpoint.

sources.supports: An access token can be used as a bearer token in authorization headers.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.

openQuestions.question: Candidate established at existence level only; format, variants, benign siblings and lifecycle are not researched.

JWT structure is only stated as "JSON Web Token". No prefix, claim names beyond scope (scp) and expiration (exp), or signing algorithm is recorded here; whether a header or claim constant exists that attributes a JWT to JFrog is unresolved.
The documentation treats tokens from OIDC exchange, identity tokens and admin tokens as access tokens. Whether any needs its own family is unresolved.

A JWT shape does not identify a JFrog access token: the same page documents that a reference token, an alias of the longer token, can be used as the password for basic authentication, so the carrier and the JWT form together do not identify the token kind. Reference tokens are the separate family jfrog:reference-token.
The pages read name no response member (such as access_token) for a newly created access token; none is recorded.
